---
title: "1.2 — Semantics: valuations and truth tables"
---

> **Where you are.** A `Form` is a tree. We now define a function that assigns it a Boolean
> value under a valuation. The final solver will use these calculations, with a proof that
> its finite table covers every valuation relevant to the formula.

## 1. The question: true under which assignment?

Take `(p ∨ q) → q`. With p true and q false it is false; with both false it is true. A formula
with atoms has a value relative to an assignment. A **valuation** is that assignment, represented
by `v : Nat → Bool`. The input is an atom index; the output is its truth value.


```lean
import Principia.Logic.Semantics
open Principia Principia.Form
open scoped Principia.Form Principia
```


```lean
def onlyFirst : Nat → Bool := fun i => i == 0
#eval onlyFirst 0  -- true
#eval onlyFirst 1  -- false
#eval eval onlyFirst ((Form.var 0 ⋎ Form.var 1) ⇒ Form.var 1)  -- false
```

These print `true`, `false`, and `false`. `fun i => ...` defines a function: given an index,
compare it with zero. It assigns false to every other index as well, so it is a complete
valuation even though we only inspect two indices here.

## 2. Reading the evaluator

The supplied `eval` has one equation per constructor:

```text
eval v (var i)   = v i
eval v falsum    = false
eval v (imp a b) = (!eval v a) || eval v b
eval v (and a b) = eval v a && eval v b
eval v (or a b)  = eval v a || eval v b
```

`!` reverses a Boolean, `&&` is Boolean and, and `||` is Boolean or. An implication is false
only when its input is true and its output false. Our concrete example evaluates as follows:

```text
p = true; q = false
p or q = true
not (p or q) = false
(not (p or q)) or q = false
```

This is structural recursion on formula data. It doesn't search for a derivation.

We can also reason with unknown children if we know enough about their values:

```lean
example (v : Nat → Bool) (a b : Form) (ha : eval v a = true) :
    eval v (a ⋎ b) = true := by
  simp only [eval]
  rw [ha]
  rfl
```

After unfolding, the goal is `(eval v a || eval v b) = true`. Rewriting `ha` turns the first
input into `true`; `true || x` computes to `true` regardless of the unknown second input.

## 3. A proposition about all valuations

We define a **tautology** to be a formula that evaluates to true under every valuation:

```lean
def Tautology (φ : Form) : Prop :=
  ∀ v, eval v φ = true
```

`Tautology` is our definition, provided in `Principia/Logic/Semantics.lean` and in your
`Skeleton.lean`; it is not a built-in Lean keyword. Read its parts as follows:

- `(φ : Form)`: its input is a formula tree.
- `: Prop`: its output is a proposition that we can try to prove.
- `∀ v`: for every valuation `v : Nat → Bool`. Lean infers this type from `eval v φ`.
- `eval v φ = true`: the formula must evaluate to true under that valuation.

Thus `eval v φ` computes one Boolean value, while `Tautology φ` claims that the value
is true for **every** possible assignment. The name `Tautology` adds no extra condition:
it abbreviates exactly the proposition on the right of `:=`.

If the goal is `Tautology φ`, `intro v` opens this universal quantifier. Lean unfolds the
definition as needed, and the proof state becomes:

```text
φ : Form
v : Nat → Bool
⊢ eval v φ = true
```

We have not chosen particular truth values: `v` is arbitrary, so the remaining proof
must work for any valuation. For example:

```lean
example (a b : Form) : Tautology ((a ⋏ b) ⇒ b) := by
  intro v
  simp only [eval]
  cases eval v a <;> cases eval v b <;> rfl
```

After `intro v`, we must prove the formula evaluates to true for this arbitrary valuation.
Unfolding leaves `(!(eval v a && eval v b) || eval v b) = true`. There are two Boolean values
to inspect, giving four cases. `rfl` computes each remaining goal. This proves validity for
arbitrary formulas a and b.

### What `<;>` does, one branch at a time

Read `firstTactic <;> nextTactic` as: **run the first tactic, then run the next tactic on
every subgoal it creates**. It is one tactic-combining operator. It doesn't choose a proof
for you: the following tactic still has to work in each branch.

In our line:

```text
cases eval v a <;> cases eval v b <;> rfl
```

1. `cases eval v a` creates two branches: its value is false or true.
2. The first `<;>` runs `cases eval v b` in **both** branches. Each splits again, giving
   the four combinations (false, false), (false, true), (true, false), and (true, true).
3. The second `<;>` runs `rfl` in **all four** branches. Each goal is now a concrete
   Boolean computation that reduces to `true = true`.

Here is the same proof with every branch written explicitly:

```lean
example (a b : Form) : Tautology ((a ⋏ b) ⇒ b) := by
  intro v
  simp only [eval]
  cases eval v a with
  | false =>
    cases eval v b with
    | false => rfl
    | true => rfl
  | true =>
    cases eval v b with
    | false => rfl
    | true => rfl
```

A newline or a plain `;` sequences tactics on the current goal; it doesn't repeat the next
tactic across the new branches. `<;>` saves that repetition when the same next step works
in each branch. If different branches need different arguments, write them separately as above.

### Entailment: what follows when assumptions are true?

`Entails` is a definition we write in Lean for this course. It is not a built-in Lean
keyword. Lean supplies `Prop`, `∀`, `→`, lists, and equality; we use them to define the
semantic claim that a conclusion follows from a list of assumptions:

```text
def Entails (Γ : List Form) (a : Form) : Prop :=
  ∀ v, (∀ b, b ∈ Γ → eval v b = true) → eval v a = true
```

`Γ` (Greek capital gamma) is simply the name of a list of formulas, such as `[a, a ⇒ b]`.
Its elements are the assumptions; `a` in the definition is the requested conclusion.
Both are formula **data**. `Entails Γ a : Prop` is the Lean proposition we state about them.

Read the definition from the outside inward:

- `∀ v`: choose any valuation `v : Nat → Bool`.
- `∀ b, b ∈ Γ → eval v b = true`: suppose every formula listed in Γ evaluates to true
  under that **same** valuation. The membership condition restricts this requirement to Γ;
  it does not assert that every possible formula is true.
- `→ eval v a = true`: under that assumption, the conclusion must also evaluate to true.

Thus a counterexample to `Entails Γ a` must make **all assumptions true and the conclusion
false at once**. A valuation making one assumption false does not meet the condition we
are investigating.

For example, `Entails [a, a ⇒ b] b` says: whenever a and “a implies b” are both true, b is
true. Here are all four combinations of their Boolean values:

| a | b | a ⇒ b | Are both assumptions true? | What does this row show? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| false | false | true | No: a is false. | Not a counterexample. |
| false | true | true | No: a is false. | Not a counterexample. |
| true | false | false | No: a ⇒ b is false. | Not a counterexample. |
| true | true | true | Yes. | The conclusion b is true. |

The row with a true and b false would refute `Entails [a] b`. It does not refute
`Entails [a, a ⇒ b] b`, because the additional implication assumption is false in that row.

We can prove the latter semantic claim directly in Lean:

```lean
example (a b : Form) : Entails [a, a ⇒ b] b := by
  intro v hΓ  -- Two introductions: intro v, then intro hΓ.
  have ha : eval v a = true := hΓ a (by simp)
  have hab : eval v (a ⇒ b) = true := hΓ (a ⇒ b) (by simp)
  simp only [eval] at hab
  rw [ha] at hab
  simp at hab
  exact hab
```

After `intro v hΓ`, the proof state is:

```text
v : Nat → Bool
hΓ : ∀ c, c ∈ [a, a ⇒ b] → eval v c = true
⊢ eval v b = true
```

The name `hΓ` is ours; its type comes from introducing the premise in the definition.
It takes a formula and evidence that the formula belongs to the list. So `hΓ a (by simp)`
supplies truth of a, and `hΓ (a ⇒ b) (by simp)` supplies truth of the implication.
Each `by simp` proves the corresponding list membership.

`at hab` tells a tactic to act on the hypothesis named `hab`. Without this location,
`simp only [eval]` simplifies the current goal; `simp only [eval] at hab` simplifies the
statement proved by `hab`. Likewise, `rw [ha] at hab` rewrites inside that hypothesis.
Here its type changes as follows, while the goal remains `eval v b = true`:

```text
hab : eval v (a ⇒ b) = true                 -- before
hab : (!eval v a || eval v b) = true        -- after simp only [eval] at hab
hab : (!true || eval v b) = true            -- after rw [ha] at hab
```

The last two lines finish in separate steps. `simp at hab` reduces `!true` to false and
`false || eval v b` to `eval v b`. Now `hab : eval v b = true`, so `exact hab` closes the goal.

You can combine those two steps here with a tactic called **`simpa`**:

```text
simpa using hab
```

`using hab` selects the proof to use. `simpa` simplifies both the goal and the statement
proved by `hab`, then checks that they match and finishes the proof. Here the goal already
has the desired form; simplifying the statement of `hab` makes it match. In this particular
Boolean example, `exact hab` also works directly after the rewrite, because Lean can compute
these reductions while checking the types. `simpa` also handles simplifications that need
proved lemmas. This is a proof of the semantic claim using Lean's own logic.

The notation `Γ ⊨ a` abbreviates `Entails Γ a`. The symbol `⇒` inside a formula builds
`Form.imp` data; the `→` in the definition above is Lean's implication between propositions.
With Γ empty, there are no assumptions to restrict the valuations, so `Entails [] a`
expresses the same claim as `Tautology a`.

## 4. Why a finite table is enough

Three supplied functions build and check a finite truth table: `maxVar` chooses its columns,
`allEnvs` builds its rows, and `taut?` checks the formula on those rows. These are definitions
in our course library, written in Lean.

### 4.1 `maxVar`: how many index positions must the table cover?

Although valuations are functions on all natural numbers, any particular formula uses only
finitely many indices. Here is the recursive definition:

```text
def maxVar : Form → Nat
  | .var n   => n + 1
  | .falsum  => 0
  | .imp a b => max (maxVar a) (maxVar b)
  | .and a b => max (maxVar a) (maxVar b)
  | .or a b  => max (maxVar a) (maxVar b)
```

For an atom at index n, we need all index positions from zero through n, so the bound is n + 1.
Falsehood contains no atoms, giving zero. At a binary node, `max` takes the larger of the
two children's bounds. It is Lean's ordinary maximum function on natural numbers.

For example:

```text
maxVar (var 0 ⋎ var 2)
  = max (maxVar (var 0)) (maxVar (var 2))
  = max 1 3
  = 3
```

Thus the table covers indices 0, 1, and 2, even though this formula never uses index 1.
`maxVar` gives an **exclusive upper bound**: every atom index is strictly smaller than it.
It does not count distinct atoms, and it does not evaluate their truth values.

```lean
#eval maxVar (Form.var 3)  -- 4
#eval maxVar (Form.var 0 ⋎ Form.var 2)  -- 3
```

### 4.2 `allEnvs`: build all assignments for those columns

An environment here is another name for a valuation, a function `Nat → Bool`.
`allEnvs n : List (Nat → Bool)` returns a list of such functions:

```text
def allEnvs : Nat → List (Nat → Bool)
  | 0 => [fun _ => false]
  | n + 1 => (allEnvs n).flatMap (fun v =>
      [v, fun k => if k == n then true else v k])
```

At zero, there are no columns to choose. There is **one** empty assignment, represented by
a function returning false everywhere. The result is a singleton list, not an empty list.

To add column n, take each existing valuation v and produce two rows:

- Keep v, which has false at the new index n.
- Create a function that returns true at n and agrees with v at every other index.

`flatMap` applies this two-row construction to each old valuation and joins the resulting
small lists into one list. Each new column doubles the number of rows, so there are $2^n$ rows.
Indices outside the selected columns keep their default value false.

For two columns, we can inspect the returned functions by applying each to indices 0 and 1:

```lean
#eval (allEnvs 0).map (fun v => [v 0, v 1])  -- [[false, false]]
#eval (allEnvs 1).map (fun v => [v 0, v 1])  -- [[false, false], [true, false]]
#eval (allEnvs 2).map (fun v => [v 0, v 1])
-- [[false, false], [false, true], [true, false], [true, true]]
```

Here `.map (fun v => [v 0, v 1])` turns each valuation into a readable pair of its outputs.
The original entries of `allEnvs` are functions; this display merely lets us see their rows.

### 4.3 `taut?`: does every generated row make the formula true?

The runnable checker is:

```text
def taut? (a : Form) : Bool :=
  (allEnvs (maxVar a)).all (fun v => eval v a)
```

Read it in three steps. First compute `maxVar a` to choose the column bound. Then construct
those rows with `allEnvs`. Finally, `List.all` applies `fun v => eval v a` to every row:
it returns true if every result is true, and false if any result is false.

For `(var 0 ⋎ var 1) ⇒ var 1`, the bound is 2. Its four rows give:

| v 0 | v 1 | v 0 or v 1 | Does the implication hold? |
|---|---|---|---|
| false | false | false | true |
| false | true | true | true |
| true | false | true | false |
| true | true | true | true |

The third row makes the implication false, so the overall check returns false:

```lean
#eval taut? ((Form.var 0 ⋎ Form.var 1) ⇒ Form.var 1)  -- false
```

`taut? a : Bool` is a computation. `Tautology a : Prop` is the claim that a evaluates to
true under **every** valuation, including functions that are not literally in our list.
The question mark is part of this checker's name; it does not turn the function into a tactic.

### 4.4 Why can these finitely many rows represent every valuation?

Two valuations that agree at the atom indices occurring in a formula give it the same value.
Values at unused indices cannot affect evaluation. For example, changing index 100 has no
effect on a formula containing only indices 0 and 1.

The generated rows cover every combination below `maxVar a`; fixing later indices at false
therefore loses no relevant case. Sparse atom indices can add redundant columns, but do not
omit any combination that matters.

The final solver uses the certified theorem
`taut?_eq_true_iff a : taut? a = true ↔ Tautology a`. Its proof connects these two facts:
evaluation ignores irrelevant indices, and the finite table represents every relevant assignment.
This justifies using the Boolean computation as evidence of the universal proposition.

### 4.5 What does the truth table decide?

Our evaluator takes a formula `a : Form` and a valuation `v : Nat → Bool`. The valuation
supplies the truth values of the atoms; `eval` then computes how the connectives combine
those values. For `a ⋎ ∼a`, there are only two possible values of `eval v a`:

| `eval v a` | `eval v (∼a)` | `eval v (a ⋎ ∼a)` |
|---|---|---|
| `false` | `true` | `true` |
| `true` | `false` | `true` |

Both rows give true. This establishes that the **formula** `a ⋎ ∼a` is a tautology,
whatever values the valuation assigns to its atoms. It does not tell us whether `a`
itself is true: the table includes both possibilities.

Now suppose we use `Form.var 0` to represent the mathematical claim “every natural number
has property P”. Our evaluator sees only an atom with index 0. If `v 0 = true`, it returns
true for that atom; if `v 0 = false`, it returns false. It never examines natural numbers
or property P. Choosing `v 0 = true` is an input assignment, not a proof of the claim.

In Lean, the actual claim would be a proposition such as `∀ n : Nat, P n`, for
`P : Nat → Prop`. There is no general algorithm that decides every such proposition.
Our finite truth-table checker does something more specific: it decides whether a formula
built from our propositional constructors evaluates to true under every assignment of
Boolean values to its atoms. It does not determine the truth of mathematical claims that
we might use those atoms to represent.

## 5. From formula trees to claims about their meaning

### 5.1 Distinguish formulas, Boolean values, and propositions

For the formula `Form.var 0 ⋎ Form.var 1`, consider a valuation assigning false to both atoms:

```lean
#eval eval (fun _ => false) (Form.var 0 ⋎ Form.var 1) -- false
```

The output is false. The relevant types have different jobs:

| Expression | Type | What it represents |
|---|---|---|
| `Form.var 0 ⋎ Form.var 1` | `Form` | A formula tree. |
| `eval (fun _ => false) (Form.var 0 ⋎ Form.var 1)` | `Bool` | Its computed value under this assignment. |
| `eval v a = true` | `Prop` | A claim about one evaluation. |
| `Tautology a` | `Prop` | A claim about every valuation. |

One true row doesn't establish a tautology. One false row is enough to refute it. Checking
that every row in a finite table is true establishes validity only once we have justified
that the table covers all relevant assignments. The final solver will use that coverage proof.

### 5.2 A transformation can come with a semantic guarantee

A function returning `Form` builds a new formula tree. Its type alone does not say how the
new formula's truth value relates to the original. We state that relation as a theorem.
For example, implication can be written using negation and disjunction:

```lean
def expandImplication (a b : Form) : Form := ∼a ⋎ b

example (v : Nat → Bool) (a b : Form) :
    eval v (expandImplication a b) = eval v (a ⇒ b) := by
  simp [expandImplication, Form.neg, eval]
```

On the left we evaluate the tree `∼a ⋎ b`; on the right we evaluate `a ⇒ b`. Both compute
`(!eval v a) || eval v b`, so they agree under any valuation. The trees are different,
but their meanings agree. This proof establishes that guarantee for arbitrary `a`, `b`, and `v`.

Other transformations change truth values in a predictable way rather than preserving them.
The final exercise explores one of these: Boolean duality. It also asks you to transform an
entire formula recursively. As in the earlier lesson on expression trees, structural induction
will give one case per constructor and hypotheses about the immediate subformulas.


```lean
theorem eval_neg (v : Nat → Bool) (φ : Form) : eval v (∼φ) = !eval v φ := by
  sorry
```

```lean
theorem taut_imp_self (φ : Form) : Tautology (φ ⇒ φ) := by
  sorry
```

```lean
theorem taut_excluded_middle (φ : Form) : Tautology (φ ⋎ ∼φ) := by
  sorry
```

### Final exercise — build a dual formula and prove its evaluation law

The **Boolean dual** exchanges conjunction and disjunction, and exchanges falsehood and
truth. Atoms keep their names. Write $D(a)$ for the dual of $a$ in this description;
your Lean function will be named `dual`.

| Input | Required output |
|---|---|
| Atom `Form.var i` | The same atom `Form.var i` |
| Falsehood `⊥` | Truth `Form.top` |
| Conjunction $a \land b$ | $D(a) \lor D(b)$ |
| Disjunction $a \lor b$ | $D(a) \land D(b)$ |
| Implication $a \to b$ | $\neg D(a) \land D(b)$ |

The implication rule follows the same idea: view $a \to b$ as $\neg a \lor b$, exchange
“or” for “and”, and dualize the subformulas while retaining the negation.
In Lean, use `∼`, `⋏`, and `⋎` for the formula connectives. `Form.top` is already defined as
`∼(⊥)`. There is no separate negation constructor: the five rows above cover every constructor
of `Form`.

For example, the dual of `Form.var 0 ⋎ Form.var 1` is `Form.var 0 ⋏ Form.var 1`.
If both atoms are true, both these formulas are true. **Duality does not simply negate a
formula's value under the same valuation.** To express its evaluation law, we also reverse
all the input values:

```lean
def flipValuation (v : Nat → Bool) : Nat → Bool := fun i => !(v i)

#eval flipValuation (fun _ => true) 0  -- false
#eval flipValuation (fun _ => false) 0 -- true
```

This function is given in the skeleton. `flipValuation v` is another valuation: wherever
`v` returns true it returns false, and vice versa. In the example with both atoms true,
the original disjunction becomes false under the flipped valuation; negating that result
gives true, exactly the dual's value under the initial valuation.

**Part A.** Implement `dual` with recursive pattern matching, following all five rules.
Use the same equation style as `eval`: remove `:= sorry` and write the five equations,
each beginning with `|`.

```lean
def dual : Form → Form :=
  sorry
```

**Part B.** Prove the following for every formula, not just a few truth-table rows:

```lean
theorem eval_dual (v : Nat → Bool) (φ : Form) :
    eval v (dual φ) = !eval (flipValuation v) φ := by
  sorry
```

Read the equality in order: evaluate the **dual** under `v`; evaluate the **original** under
`flipValuation v`, then negate that Boolean result. The `!` acts on a `Bool`, whereas `∼`
builds a negated `Form`. You will need structural induction on `φ` to cover every formula.

The required status determines whether the lab succeeds. Optional placeholders are reported
separately in yellow when terminal colors are available; required success is green.

## 7. Hints

**`eval_neg`.** Unfold the definition of formula negation and the evaluation equations. A Boolean or with false can be simplified.

**`taut_imp_self`.** Introduce an arbitrary valuation. After unfolding, split on the Boolean value of the subformula.

**`taut_excluded_middle`.** Introduce a valuation and unfold formula negation as well as evaluation. Consider the two Boolean values of the subformula.

**`dual`.** Match on the five constructors, as in `eval`. For a binary constructor,
recursively transform both children before combining the results. The implication case
changes the outer connective too; copying an implication with transformed children does
not implement the specified dual.

**`eval_dual`.** Start with `induction φ with`. For an atom, unfold `flipValuation` and
use Boolean double negation; for falsehood, both sides compute. Each binary case has two
induction hypotheses. Unfold the outer evaluation, rewrite the evaluations of the dual
children with those hypotheses, then inspect the two Boolean values
`eval (flipValuation v) a` and `eval (flipValuation v) b`. This leaves four computational
cases, like the Boolean proofs in the lesson.

## 8. Worked corrections to the required exercises

Try the exercises first. These proofs match `Solution.lean`, checked by `make test`.

### `eval_neg`

```lean
theorem eval_neg (v : Nat → Bool) (φ : Form) : eval v (∼φ) = !eval v φ := by
  simp [Form.neg, eval]
```

Negation expands to implication into falsehood. Unfolding leaves a Boolean negation combined with false, and simplification uses the Boolean identity.

### `taut_imp_self`

```lean
theorem taut_imp_self (φ : Form) : Tautology (φ ⇒ φ) := by
  intro v; simp only [eval]; cases eval v φ <;> rfl
```

The arbitrary valuation is introduced by the universal quantifier in `Tautology`. The remaining claim depends on one Boolean value. The two branches compute to true.

### `taut_excluded_middle`

```lean
theorem taut_excluded_middle (φ : Form) : Tautology (φ ⋎ ∼φ) := by
  intro v; simp only [eval, Form.neg]; cases eval v φ <;> rfl
```

The proof again checks a Boolean value, after exposing the derived negation. It proves semantic validity of formula syntax, without deciding arbitrary Lean propositions.

### `dual` and `eval_dual`

The supplied `flipValuation` above is used by this solution:

```lean
def dual : Form → Form
  | .var i => .var i
  | .falsum => Form.top
  | .imp a b => ∼(dual a) ⋏ dual b
  | .and a b => dual a ⋎ dual b
  | .or a b => dual a ⋏ dual b

theorem eval_dual (v : Nat → Bool) (φ : Form) :
    eval v (dual φ) = !eval (flipValuation v) φ := by
  induction φ with
  | var i => simp [dual, eval, flipValuation]
  | falsum => rfl
  | imp a b ihA ihB =>
    simp only [dual, Form.neg, eval]
    rw [ihA, ihB]
    cases eval (flipValuation v) a <;> cases eval (flipValuation v) b <;> rfl
  | and a b ihA ihB =>
    simp only [dual, eval]
    rw [ihA, ihB]
    cases eval (flipValuation v) a <;> cases eval (flipValuation v) b <;> rfl
  | or a b ihA ihB =>
    simp only [dual, eval]
    rw [ihA, ihB]
    cases eval (flipValuation v) a <;> cases eval (flipValuation v) b <;> rfl
```

In `var`, the goal says that `v i` equals its double Boolean negation. In `falsum`,
the dual is truth, while the right side is `!false`.

Consider the `and` branch in more detail. The two induction hypotheses have types:

```text
ihA : eval v (dual a) = !eval (flipValuation v) a
ihB : eval v (dual b) = !eval (flipValuation v) b
```

After unfolding and rewriting, the goal is a Boolean De Morgan law. If we abbreviate
`eval (flipValuation v) a` by `x` and the corresponding value of `b` by `y`, it reads:

```text
(!x || !y) = !(x && y)
```

Splitting on `x` and `y` checks all four possibilities. The `or` branch uses the other
De Morgan law; the implication branch checks the rule for implication in the same way.
You can always split on `eval v a` with `cases`: its result is a `Bool`, so the two
branches cover every possible value. However, splitting on one evaluation does not by
itself establish its relation to another evaluation. Here we need to relate
`eval v (dual a)` to `eval (flipValuation v) a`. Knowing that the second is false does
not yet tell Lean that the first is true.

That connection comes from `ihA`: it says the first evaluation is the Boolean negation
of the second. The proof therefore has two steps with different roles:

1. `rw [ihA, ihB]` replaces the evaluations of the dual children using the relations
   supplied by the induction hypotheses.
2. The two `cases` commands inspect the remaining Boolean values. The resulting four
   branches compute with `rfl`.

These case splits concern arbitrary subformulas `a` and `b`, so they cover both possible
values regardless of the subformulas' shapes. This is different from running `#eval` on
a few particular formula trees, which would check only those examples.

Use `optional/Skeleton.lean`; the same lab command checks it separately. These exercises have
their own verified answer key in `optional/Solution.lean`.

```lean
theorem eval_top (v : Nat → Bool) : eval v Form.top = true := by
  sorry
```

*Hint:* Expand top, formula negation, and evaluation. No atom lookup remains.


```lean
theorem taut_and_elim_left (a b : Form) : Tautology ((a ⋏ b) ⇒ a) := by
  sorry
```

*Hint:* Introduce an arbitrary valuation, then inspect the two child values.


Read each statement as an input/output contract. Identify what evidence is already available
and what result must be built. You may reuse the proved library results from this lesson.

## 10. Worked corrections to the optional exercises

### `eval_top`

```lean
theorem eval_top (v : Nat → Bool) : eval v Form.top = true := by
  simp [Form.top, Form.neg, eval]
```

`top` is negated falsehood, so unfolding gives `(!false) || false`, which computes to true. This statement holds under any valuation because no atom occurs in the formula.


### `taut_and_elim_left`

```lean
theorem taut_and_elim_left (a b : Form) : Tautology ((a ⋏ b) ⇒ a) := by
  intro v
  simp only [eval]
  cases eval v a <;> cases eval v b <;> rfl
```

After introducing v, evaluation leaves `(!(eval v a && eval v b) || eval v a) = true`. The two `cases` commands create the four combinations of the subformula values. Each remaining goal computes. This is the left projection, different from the right projection in the teaching example.


## 11. Conclusion

A valuation supplies Boolean inputs, `eval` combines them, and `Tautology` quantifies over
all valuations. A formula has finitely many relevant indices even though valuations are functions
on every index. The finite table is executable; its certified equivalence will support the solver.
The duality exercise adds a different use of semantics: specify how a transformation changes
a formula's meaning, then prove that specification for every input tree. Structural recursion
builds the transformation; structural induction proves its evaluation law.

Next we define derivations, keeping semantic truth separate from proof construction.
